that something more fundamental than per-post throttling was going on.

Ruled out the two live hypotheses methodically rather than picking one:
tried single-metric requests (isolating whether one bad metric name in a
batched request was silently zeroing the whole response -- it wasn't),
confirmed the video IDs themselves resolve fine via basic `/{video_id}
?fields=id,length,status` calls (so it's not a bad-ID problem), and
discovered along the way that the post-level `/{post_id}/insights` edge
hard-errors for Reels post_ids specifically (`(#12) singular statuses API
is deprecated for versions v2.4 and higher` -- a known Graph API quirk:
Reels post_ids don't behave like classic Page post_ids for this edge, so
that path is a dead end for this content type regardless of anything
else).

**Root cause, confirmed directly**: `GET /{page_id}?fields=fan_count,
followers_count` returned **10 and 10**. The Core Decor Facebook Page has
10 followers. Meta suppresses Page/video Insights data below a documented
minimum audience threshold (100+ likes for standard Page Insights,
consistent with the uniformly-empty video_insights results regardless of
post age). This fully explains the empty insights data on its own, with
no need to invoke throttling, API-vs-native publishing, or anything
Reels-specific -- a page with 10 followers has almost no organic reach
on ANY platform through ANY publishing method. The original "is the API
being throttled" question was chasing the wrong variable; the real
constraint is that the Facebook Page's own audience is essentially
unbuilt, disconnected from whatever audience Instagram/TikTok/YouTube
have. Growing Facebook reach here is an audience-building problem, not a
pipeline or publishing-method bug -- no code fix addresses it.

Three small reusable diagnostic/recovery workflows came out of this,
all `workflow_dispatch`-only (never scheduled), safe to keep:
- `publish-existing-to-facebook.yml` -- publish an already-hosted
  video+caption to Facebook directly, for recovering a post that's
  missing from FB without regenerating content or touching rotation
  counters.
- `check-facebook-video-insights.yml` -- pull real video_insights /
  post-level insights / basic fields for given video_id(s)/post_id(s).
- `check-facebook-page-followers.yml` -- pull the Page's own fan_count/
  followers_count directly.

## Vertex AI Imagen setup for the new e-series (2026-08-22) -- gcloud commands Dev needs to run

Dev is setting up Google's Imagen (via Vertex AI) for a new "e-series" content
type that copies the format of viral reels he'll upload to a new Drive folder
("E-Series Reference Reels", nested under ROOT_FOLDER_ID -- see
create-eseries-folder.yml). Chose Google's models specifically for the $300
new-GCP-account trial credit.

**Critical gotcha confirmed via a live web check, not assumed**: the $300 credit
covers Vertex AI/Imagen (billed through an actual GCP billing account) but
explicitly does NOT cover the separate Gemini Developer API (an AI Studio key) --
Google carved that out on purpose. Getting this wrong means burning real money
on a key type the promo credit doesn't touch. Also: the "Vertex AI" console
itself was renamed/folded into "Gemini Enterprise" as of a May 2026 rebrand --
same underlying service, different name, worth knowing before hunting for a
UI that no longer exists under its old name.

Dev pasted setup advice from elsewhere that got two real things wrong and
missed one step entirely:
- Called `generate_content()` with a Claude model (`claude-3-5-sonnet@...`) --
  Claude IS available via Vertex Model Garden, but that's irrelevant here;
  image generation needs `generate_images()` with an Imagen model instead.
- Used a bare `genai.Client()` with no arguments, which defaults to the
  Gemini Developer API (not covered by the credit) rather than Vertex AI
  billing. Needs `genai.Client(vertexai=True, project=..., location=...)`.
- The 4 gcloud commands it gave only set up Workload Identity Federation
  *authentication* (letting the GitHub Actions OIDC token impersonate the
  service account) -- never granted that service account actual *permission*
  to call Vertex AI. Without a 5th command granting `roles/aiplatform.user`,
  every real request would 403 even after auth succeeds.

The WIF approach itself (no static service-account key, short-lived tokens via
`google-github-actions/auth@v2`) is correct and current -- kept that part,
fixed the rest. `.github/workflows/test-vertex-imagen.yml` is the corrected,
ready-to-run connectivity test (workflow_dispatch only, generates one
throwaway image as a build artifact, not wired into any content pipeline).

**Dev's real GCP project details** (from what he already ran/received):
project_id `project-58f4f689-36b9-406b-bfa`, project_number `584573644858`.
Already baked into test-vertex-imagen.yml's `workload_identity_provider` and
`service_account` fields.

**Exact commands Dev needs to run in Cloud Shell** (his own GCP identity required
-- Claude has no gcloud CLI access in this sandbox and couldn't run these even
if it did, since IAM changes need the project owner's own credentials):

```bash
PROJECT_ID="project-58f4f689-36b9-406b-bfa"
PROJECT_NUMBER="584573644858"
REPO="devdave666/core-decor-automation"

# 1. Workload Identity Pool
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create "github-pool" \
  --project="$PROJECT_ID" --location="global" \
  --display-name="GitHub Actions Pool"

# 2. OIDC Provider for GitHub
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc "github-provider" \
  --project="$PROJECT_ID" --location="global" \
  --workload-identity-pool="github-pool" \
  --display-name="GitHub Actions Provider" \
  --attribute-mapping="google.subject=assertion.sub,attribute.actor=assertion.actor,attribute.repository=assertion.repository" \
  --issuer-uri="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"

# 3. Service account (if vertex-ai-runner doesn't already exist)
gcloud iam service-accounts create "vertex-ai-runner" \
  --project="$PROJECT_ID" --display-name="Vertex AI Runner for GitHub Actions"

# 4. Let this specific GitHub repo impersonate the service account
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \
  "vertex-ai-runner@${PROJECT_ID}.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
  --project="$PROJECT_ID" --role="roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser" \
  --member="principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/${PROJECT_NUMBER}/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/github-pool/attribute.repository/${REPO}"

# 5. THE MISSING STEP -- actually grant Vertex AI access (without this, auth
#    succeeds but every real Imagen call 403s)
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding "$PROJECT_ID" \
  --member="serviceAccount:vertex-ai-runner@${PROJECT_ID}.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
  --role="roles/aiplatform.user"
```

Once run, Dev triggers `test-vertex-imagen.yml` via workflow_dispatch himself
(or asks Claude to). Success = a real generated image in the run's build
artifacts. Only once that's confirmed working should any actual e-series
generation script get built against this -- no point designing the real
pipeline against an untested auth chain.

**Still blocked on**: (1) Dev running the 5 commands above, (2) Dev uploading
example viral reels to the new Drive folder for format analysis. Neither
happened yet as of this entry.

## WIF setup, continued: attribute-condition now required + Dev wants single point of contact (2026-08-22)

Dev ran the 5 commands from the entry above in his own Cloud Shell (his own
identity required -- confirmed this is a hard boundary, not something to
route around: Claude has no gcloud CLI in this sandbox, and IAM-Admin-level
project changes need the project owner's own credentials, which handing to
Claude would defeat the actual point of using WIF over a static key).

Results: pool created successfully. Service account creation "failed"
harmlessly (`vertex-ai-runner` already existed from an earlier attempt --
not a real problem, nothing to redo). Both IAM bindings (workloadIdentityUser
on the service account, aiplatform.user on the project) succeeded and are
confirmed live via the real `gcloud` output Dev pasted back, not assumed.

Only the OIDC provider creation failed: `INVALID_ARGUMENT: The attribute
condition must reference one of the provider's claims`. Root cause confirmed
via search, not guessed: recent `gcloud` versions require an explicit
`--attribute-condition` flag on GitHub Actions WIF providers -- a real
Google security tightening (prevents an unscoped trust boundary from being
created by accident), not a mistake in the original advice's command syntax
itself, just a missing flag that's become mandatory. Fix: add
`--attribute-condition="assertion.repository == 'devdave666/core-decor-automation'"`
(references the same `assertion.repository` claim already present in
`--attribute-mapping`) -- this also happens to be the more secure version
of what was being built anyway, scoping trust to exactly this one repo
rather than leaving it open.

**Standing feedback, worth remembering for future sessions on this project**:
Dev pushed back on being handed multi-step instruction sets to execute and
self-debug -- said explicitly "you need to be my single point of contact."
For anything Claude technically CAN execute (workflow_dispatch triggers,
reading logs, diagnosing failures), Claude should own it end-to-end rather
than making Dev the hands-and-eyes. The one hard exception is genuine
IAM-Admin-on-Dev's-own-GCP-project actions -- those need Dev's own identity
by design, and no amount of tooling changes that. When a step like that is
unavoidable, the right move is: give exactly ONE corrected command (not a
batch to debug), explain clearly why it's Dev's hands only for that one
step, and then take back full ownership of every step after it.

Status: waiting on Dev to run the corrected provider command above, then
Claude triggers test-vertex-imagen.yml directly and reports the real result
-- no further instructions to Dev needed for that part.

## Vertex AI image generation: confirmed working end-to-end (2026-08-22/23)

Continuation of the entries above. After the WIF attribute-condition fix, the
connectivity test still failed twice more -- each time a real, informative
failure, not noise:

1. `imagen-4.0-generate-001` -> 404. Root cause: Imagen's `generate_images()`
   models were retired (a real platform change, confirmed by the error itself,
   not assumed).
2. `gemini-2.5-flash-image-preview` -> 404. Turned out to be a wrong guess at
   the exact identifier, not a real access problem -- see below.
3. A manual `google.auth.default()` + `creds.refresh()` attempt to list the
   real catalog (to stop guessing model names blind) failed with a DIFFERENT
   error: `Unable to acquire impersonated credentials ... INVALID_ARGUMENT`
   -- an IAM impersonation scope issue in that specific hand-rolled auth path,
   unrelated to Vertex/Imagen access itself (the genai client's own auth had
   already proven working by this point, since attempts 1-2 got real 404s
   from the real API, not auth errors). Fixed by reusing the SAME
   already-authenticated `genai.Client` to list models instead of building a
   second parallel credential path: `client.models.list(config=
   {'query_base': True})`.

**Confirmed working, real generated image downloaded and visually verified**:
model `gemini-2.5-flash-image` (no `-preview` suffix -- that suffix was the
actual bug in attempt 2, not a retired/inaccessible model). The project's
publisher-model catalog returns ~20 models matching "image" in the name, but
most are non-generative (imageclassification-*, imagesegmentation-*,
imageobjectdetection-*, automl-vision-*, imagewatermarkdetector) and correctly
fail with 400s when asked to generate_content. `discover_and_test_image_model.py`
now tries `gemini-2.5-flash-image` first (confirmed fast path) before falling
back to the full discovered list, so a normal run doesn't burn through ~13
irrelevant candidates first.

WIF auth, IAM permissions (`roles/aiplatform.user`), and Vertex AI billing
routing (via `vertexai=True` + project/location, not the separate Gemini
Developer API) are now all confirmed working end-to-end via a real image
successfully generated and downloaded from a real GitHub Actions run --
not just "auth succeeded," a full round trip verified by eye.

**Still blocked on**: Dev uploading example viral reels to the "E-Series
Reference Reels" Drive folder for format analysis (see the entry above with
the folder link). The Google Cloud / image-generation side is now fully
ready and does not need any further setup before the real e-series
generation script gets built -- once reels are analyzed and a concrete
format/prompt approach is proposed, `gemini-2.5-flash-image` via
`generate_content()` (same pattern as `discover_and_test_image_model.py`,
not `generate_images()`/Imagen) is what that script should call.

## E-Series: first themed set generated and validated (2026-08-22/23)

Dev uploaded real reference reels (a Drive folder literally named "Type 1 -
firstchair", 3 real mp4s) and asked for format analysis followed directly by
generation -- application photos only for now, swatches deferred to a later
decision, and asked that concept naming make the source "type" legible in
future actual reel videos, not just in a manifest.

**Format analysis, not guessed from the name alone**: downloaded all 3
reference videos and ran them through `extract_template_cut_timestamps()` --
the SAME scene-detection already trusted for the main pipeline/Dolly Reel/
Hot Takes, not a new method -- plus ffprobe metadata and 8 evenly-spaced
frames per video (`analyze_reference_reels.py`, a new reusable diagnostic
workflow). All 3: 720x1280 (9:16), 30fps, ~9-11s, AAC audio, 4-9 hard cuts
each at roughly 1-2s per segment (video 2 was cleanly 2.0s per cut, videos 1
and 3 closer to 1.1-1.3s). Frames confirmed the actual format: a rapid-cut
montage through SEVERAL DIFFERENT ROOMS of one home, all sharing ONE
cohesive material/colour palette, with a SINGLE static caption overlaid for
the entire reel naming the theme/hook ("homes with earthy tones>", "what I
mean when I say I love earthy tones:", "proof the 1960s built homes
better"). Structurally different from every existing content type here --
one THEMED SET of rooms per concept, not one room per concept, because
palette cohesion across rooms is the entire hook.

**Naming decided and applied**: `e{type}-{set:02d}` (e.g. `e1-01` = e-series,
Type 1 format, first themed set) so the source viral-reel type is legible
directly from the concept id itself. Room files within a set keep the
existing room-abbreviation convention (`e1-01_liv_app.png`,
`e1-01_din_app.png`, `e1-01_off_app.png`). Future "Type 2" (Dev's own words:
"actually has multiple concepts of reels" within it) gets `e2-01`, `e2-02`,
etc. once its own reference folder is analyzed.

**Generator built**: `concept_tools/generate_eseries.py`, run via
`.github/workflows/generate-eseries.yml` (workflow_dispatch, WIF-authenticated,
same pattern as the Vertex AI connectivity test). Deliberately reuses the
hard-tuned `COMPOSITION`/`STYLING_RULE`/`SPATIAL_RULE`/`QUALITY_ROOM`/
`NO_TEXT`/`ROOM_LIGHT` constants from `generate_concept.py` rather than
duplicating that prompt-engineering work -- `ROOM_LIGHT` in particular is
Dev's own validated house lighting style (warm-lamps-against-blue-hour, see
the extensive measured-luminance tuning notes already in `generate_concept.py`),
kept deliberately even though the reference reels themselves lean more
daytime-lit -- matching Dev's own established visual identity is the
"creative twist" applied on top of the borrowed format, not a mismatch to
fix. Swapped per-room `materials_sentence`+`bands` for one `palette_sentence`
shared across every room in a themed set, since palette cohesion IS the
format here.

Uses `gemini-2.5-flash-image` (confirmed model from the entries above),
requesting `types.GenerateContentConfig(image_config=types.ImageConfig(
aspect_ratio="9:16"))` -- unverified guess at this exact config shape going
in, confirmed to have SOME real effect (output came back 768x1344, portrait,
vs. the earlier no-config test's more square output) though not landing on
an exact 9:16 ratio. Close enough to use as-is; revisit if a later SDK
version exposes a cleaner way to hit the exact ratio.

**First set (`e1-01`, "earthy tones" -- burnt terracotta plaster, olive
velvet, walnut/smoked oak, aged brass, cream boucle/linen) generated and
reviewed by eye, not just "the script ran"**: living room, dining room,
home office, all at `assets/application_eseries/`. Confirmed genuinely
cohesive across all three -- same palette, same blue-hour-plus-warm-lamps
mood, same camera height/composition -- reads as one real home, which is
the entire point of this format. Checked each for the same geometry
failure modes flagged in the d06 postmortem (interpenetrating solids,
blocked walkways) -- clean in all three. `pillow` had to be added to the
generation workflow's dependencies (missed on the first run:
`generate_concept.py` imports PIL at module level for its own swatch/OCR
tooling, which generate_eseries.py pulls in just for the prompt constants).

**Deliberately NOT yet built**: the actual reel video assembly (cutting
these room photos to the analyzed cut-timing pattern, adding the
persistent single-caption overlay). Dev asked for "application reels ...
after analysis" -- read as "build reels using application photos, no
swatches," not "stop at still images" -- but going further without
showing the still images first risked compounding a wrong assumption
across a whole video-assembly build. Waiting on Dev's sign-off on this
first set's visual style before building that piece, which would reuse
`build_hot_take()`'s general shape (beat-synced montage, static text
overlay) from `hot_takes_pipeline.py` as its starting point, adapted for
a single persistent caption instead of a two-line reveal, and application
images that don't repeat the way Hot Takes' rotating single-photo pool
does.

Only 1 of Dev's 2 example reel "types" is uploaded/analyzed so far (Type 1).
Type 2 ("multiple concepts of reels" per Dev, not yet uploaded) will need
its own `analyze_reference_reels.py` pass and its own `e2-*` naming once it
arrives.

## Transformation Reel -- a THIRD, separate new format: Veo-generated (2026-08-22/23)

**Not the e-series above.** The e-series is a rapid-cut montage through several
ALREADY-FINISHED rooms sharing one palette. This is a completely different
content shape: ONE room, shown transforming from derelict to finished, with
human tradespeople visible mid-renovation, as an actual generated VIDEO (not
stitched stills) -- "beat-down place transforms into a high-end furnished
space, workers finishing the job" per Dev's request in a separate chat. Lives
entirely in `transformation_reel/`, nothing shared with `concept_tools/` or
the e-series generator. workflow_dispatch only, nothing committed to repo
assets, nothing wired into publishing -- proof-of-concept status only, same as
the e-series was before Dev's sign-off.

**Why three images, not two, and two chained Veo calls, not one.** Veo caps a
single first/last-frame generation at 8 seconds (confirmed via Google's own
docs), so a 15s reel needs two generations, not one. Using a THIRD "mid" frame
(workers actively renovating) as the shared midpoint -- clip A: before->mid,
clip B: mid->after -- both makes "workers finishing the transformation"
actually visible mid-reel (a single before->after generation would show the
transformation but never show anyone doing it) and keeps the two clips
continuous with each other rather than reading as two unrelated pairs.

**Frame generation (`transformation_reel/generate_concept_frames.py`,
`.github/workflows/generate-transformation-concept.yml`)**: uses
`gemini-2.5-flash-image` (the confirmed e-series/Imagen-path model, not BFL
FLUX -- this format was built following the e-series' tooling direction, not
the c/d-series'). Chained generation, not three independent prompts: "after"
(finished, styled) is generated first from text, then "before" and "mid" are
each generated by handing the model the prior image(s) directly in
`contents=[prompt, PIL.Image, ...]` alongside an edit instruction. This is the
same reason `concept_tools/edit_room.py` hands FLUX an `input_image` instead of
re-rolling from scratch -- architecture, camera angle and window/doorway
positions have to MATCH across all three for Veo's frame conditioning to read
as one continuous space. **Confirmed working on the first real concept
(`t01`, a living room with a floor-to-ceiling window wall, city skyline and a
fireplace)**: all three images reviewed by eye, architecture genuinely
identical across all three -- same windows, same skyline, same fireplace
position -- derelict (exposed wiring, cracked plaster, dust sheet) -> mid
(three workers: one painting from a ladder, one framing built-in cabinetry by
the fireplace, one at a miter saw, tools and materials staged on drop cloths)
-> after (styled, warm-lit, fire lit, furnished). The chained-edit approach
earns its complexity here; it would have been pure luck for three independent
generations to agree on window count or fireplace position.

**Veo connectivity -- confirmed via a live call, not assumed, same discipline
as the Imagen setup.** `discover_and_test_video_model.py` +
`.github/workflows/test-vertex-veo.yml` query this project's own
publisher-model catalog rather than guessing a model string (the Imagen setup
already got burned twice guessing). Result: **only the Veo 3.1 family is
enabled for this project** -- `veo-3.1-generate-001` (confirmed working),
`veo-3.1-fast-generate-001`, `veo-3.1-lite-generate-001` all appear in the
catalog; `veo-2.0-generate-001`, `veo-3.0-generate-001` and
`veo-3.0-fast-generate-001` all 404 despite being real model names elsewhere.
No new IAM was needed -- the existing `roles/aiplatform.user` grant on
`vertex-ai-runner` (set up for Imagen) already covers Veo; it's the same
Vertex Generative AI API surface. Video bytes come back inline
(`operation.response.generated_videos[0].video.video_bytes`) when no
`output_gcs_uri` is set in `GenerateVideosConfig` -- same "bytes in the
response if you don't ask for GCS" pattern the image model already uses via
`inline_data`. **No GCS bucket exists or is needed for this project.**

**Clip generation (`transformation_reel/generate_veo_clips.py`,
`.github/workflows/generate-transformation-veo-clips.yml`)**: two 8s
`generate_videos` calls with `image=<start>`, `config.last_frame=<end>`,
`generate_audio=True`, `aspect_ratio="9:16"`, then ffmpeg's concat FILTER
(re-encoding, not the stream-copy concat demuxer -- two independent Veo
generations aren't guaranteed to share encoding params, and this project
already learned the concatenation-is-dangerous lesson once for real with the
Facebook Reels truncation bug; don't assume stream-copy concat is safe just
because it's simpler).

**ASMR audio**: no separate SFX-licensing decision was made -- Veo 3.1
generates synced audio natively in the same pass, so both clips are generated
with an explicit prompt asking for "close, tactile, ASMR-style renovation
sound design ... no music, no voiceover." Confirmed the resulting track is
real and dynamic (`ffmpeg -af volumedetect`: mean -33dB, max -2.5dB, clearly
not silent or flat) but **not yet confirmed by ear that it actually reads as
ASMR-quality** -- that's a real open item, not resolved. If it turns out
insufficient on a real listen, the fallback is a licensed/generated SFX layer
mixed in during the ffmpeg concat step, but don't reach for that without
actually listening first.

**A real bug already hit and fixed, worth not repeating**: the first real run
of `generate-transformation-veo-clips.yml` generated BOTH Veo clips
successfully (i.e., paid for them, ~$10-12) and then failed at the ffmpeg
concat step because `ffmpeg` isn't preinstalled on the `ubuntu-latest` runner
-- and the upload-artifact step never ran, so both paid clips were thrown away
with nothing to show for the spend. Fixed two ways, both worth keeping on any
future workflow that spends real money before a local post-processing step:
install `ffmpeg` explicitly (`sudo apt-get install -y ffmpeg`), and put
`if: always()` on the artifact upload so a downstream failure can never again
discard output that already cost real money to produce.

**Cost, stated plainly**: Veo with audio runs roughly $0.75/s on Vertex AI, so
two 8s clips is on the order of $10-12 per successful run. This exploration
cost roughly $20-24 total (one run lost to the ffmpeg bug above, one
successful run) plus negligible image-generation cost for the three frames.
**Don't re-run `generate-transformation-veo-clips.yml` casually** -- it's
workflow_dispatch-only on purpose, same as every other paid-generation
workflow in this repo.

**Result, `t01`**: a real 16.0s, 720x1280, h264+aac video, downloaded and
reviewed frame-by-frame, not just "the job succeeded." The transformation arc
is genuinely visible and the architecture stays consistent end to end --
same window wall and skyline in the first frame, mid-renovation frames, and
final frame. This is a real, working proof of concept for the format Dev
asked about, sitting only as a GitHub Actions build artifact (not committed to
the repo -- this is unreviewed, experimental content, same staging discipline
as `concept_review/` for the c/d-series before anything gets promoted).

**Explicitly NOT done yet, and not to be assumed done**:
- **Dev has not reviewed or approved this concept or format.** Nothing here
  should be treated as validated the way the approved d-series concepts are.
- Real Instagram-viral-transformation-format research (separate from Dev's own
  uploaded e-series reference reels) found: transformation reels get roughly
  6x the average save rate on Instagram, the winning transition style is a
  "swipe wipe" cut at the before/after boundary, hook text lands in the first
  1-2 seconds, and 15-20s is the length "sweet spot" for this kind of
  high-velocity content in 2026 (this reel's 16.0s already lands inside that
  window, which is a coincidence worth confirming rather than assuming holds
  for future concepts). **None of this has been applied yet** -- there is no
  text overlay, no caption, no hook on the current `t01` output at all.
- No reel-assembly/publishing pipeline exists for this format, matching where
  the e-series was before its own video-assembly step got built. Wiring this
  into anything real needs Dev's sign-off on both the visual concept and the
  audio, the same two-part review the e-series is waiting on.
- `client.models.generate_videos`'s `prompt=`/`image=` keyword-argument form
  triggered a deprecation warning in this project's real run ("will be removed
  in a future major release (not before 2026-07-31)" -- that date has already
  passed as of this writing, though the old form still worked in the actual
  run tested here). Should move to the SDK's newer `source=
  types.GenerateVideosSource(...)` form before this becomes load-bearing in
  any real pipeline; not urgent while this stays a proof of concept, but don't
  let it linger once this gets built out for real.

## Why e-series images look lower quality than FLUX -- root cause confirmed (2026-08-23)

Dev asked directly why the Gemini-generated e-series images looked lower
quality than the a-d series' FLUX output. Answered with real measurements
and real API tests, not a general "different model" hand-wave:

**Real, measurable resolution gap**: FLUX room shots render at 1088x1920
(~2.1MP, `ROOM_W`/`ROOM_H` in `generate_concept.py`). The e-series test
image came back 768x1344 (~1.03MP) -- roughly half the pixel count. That
alone is a real, sufficient explanation for looking softer at the same
display size, before any discussion of model "quality" as a vibe.

**Tried the documented fix, it didn't work**: `image_size="4K"` is a real,
correctly-named field -- confirmed by introspecting `types.ImageConfig`'s
actual Pydantic schema directly in a throwaway workflow rather than trust
another secondhand doc summary (worth doing after `image_size` from search
results turned out to come with invented `client.interactions.create()`
syntax that doesn't match this SDK at all). The field accepts `1K`/`2K`/`4K`,
default `1K`. Requesting `4K` produced a byte-identical 768x1344 output to
the default -- silently ignored, not erroring, meaning `gemini-2.5-flash-
image` doesn't actually honor this control despite the SDK accepting it.

**Checked for a higher-tier model rather than assume none exists**: the
publisher-model catalog scanned earlier (see the "confirmed working end-to-
end" entry above) had returned 20 image-related models, but the discovery
script stopped at the first one that worked (`gemini-2.5-flash-image`) and
never tried the rest. Went back and checked what else was in that list:
`gemini-3-pro-image`, `gemini-3.1-flash-image`, `gemini-3.1-flash-image-
preview`, `gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image` were all present. Tried the two
most likely candidates for real (`gemini-3-pro-image`, the actual "Pro"
tier closer to FLUX's positioning; `gemini-3.1-flash-image`) -- both 404
with "not found or your project does not have access to it." These exist
in Google's global catalog but this specific trial project isn't allowlisted
for the Gemini 3 image family. `gemini-3-pro-image` most likely being where
`image_size` actually does something -- the docs phrase that was fetched
earlier said "Gemini 3 image models," not Gemini 2.5 -- but unconfirmed
since it's inaccessible from this account right now.

**Bottom line, stated plainly rather than softened**: `gemini-2.5-flash-
image` is the only generative image model this GCP account currently has
real access to, and it appears hard-capped around ~1MP output regardless
of requested config -- a genuine model/tier limitation, not something more
prompt tuning or parameter guessing fixes from this side. Options going
forward: (1) accept it -- may matter less in a heavily-compressed fast-cut
Reel than as a full-size still image; (2) post-process upscale (sharper-
looking, not more real detail); (3) request/wait for Gemini 3 image family
access on this GCP project; (4) fall back to FLUX for e-series too,
trading away the promo-credit cost rationale. Left `--model` override
capability in `generate_eseries.py`/`generate-eseries.yml` specifically so
testing Gemini 3 later (once/if access clears) needs zero new code.

## Transformation Reel: v2 fixes (real runs) + v3 prep for future runs (2026-08-23)

Continuation of the "Transformation Reel" entry above (t01, Veo-generated
before/mid/after). Two more real, run-and-verified iterations happened after
Dev reviewed the first output, then a third round of changes was made and
**deliberately left un-run** per Dev's explicit instruction ("do not create
anything right now ... for future reels only").

**v2, three real bugs found by Dev watching the actual output, all fixed and
re-verified against real generated video:**

1. **Workers looked sped up.** Root cause was literal: the v1 motion prompt
   said "time-lapse-style," which is exactly the effect it produced. Fixed by
   removing that phrase everywhere and adding explicit real-time/not-sped-up
   language, plus widening from 3 keyframes (before/mid/after, 2x8s clips) to
   5 keyframes (before/demo/framing/finishing/after, 4x4s clips) so each Veo
   generation only has to bridge one small step instead of a large jump --
   compounds with the prompt fix.
2. **Aspect ratio was wrong, and it took TWO fixes to actually resolve.**
   First finding: `gemini-2.5-flash-image` needs `GenerateContentConfig(
   image_config=ImageConfig(aspect_ratio=...))` as a real config param --
   requesting "vertical 9:16" in prompt TEXT alone (v1's approach) does
   nothing. Fixed that, regenerated, and the STILL images came back properly
   portrait (768x1344) -- but the real generated VEO CLIPS still came back
   letterboxed. Second finding, confirmed by extracting real video frames and
   checking pixel dimensions with PIL (not assumed): 768x1344 (ratio 0.5714)
   is close to but NOT identical to Veo's own real output canvas of 720x1280
   (ratio 0.5625, confirmed via ffprobe on a generated clip) -- Veo pads that
   small mismatch with black bars rather than cropping to fill. Fixed by
   center-cropping every source frame to exactly 720x1280 via `ImageOps.fit`
   immediately after generation (`VEO_CANVAS` in `generate_concept_frames.py`),
   so the mismatch never reaches Veo. Confirmed genuinely fixed by re-checking
   pixel content of a newly generated real clip -- full-bleed, no black bars,
   on every sampled frame.
3. **Wrong tier/cost for iterating on visuals.** Switched from
   `veo-3.1-generate-001` (Standard, audio-on, ~$0.75/s) to
   `veo-3.1-lite-generate-001` (audio off, ~$0.05/s) specifically to make the
   above two rounds of iteration cheap while the VISUALS were still being
   fixed -- not a permanent decision, see v3 below.

Also hit and fixed along the way: a 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED on
`gemini-2.5-flash-image` after widening to 5 chained calls per concept
(exponential backoff added, `MAX_RETRIES=5`), and a missing `pillow` install
in `generate-transformation-veo-clips.yml` (needed transitively --
`generate_veo_clips.py` now imports `STAGES` from `generate_concept_frames.py`,
which imports PIL at module level; same class of bug the e-series build above
already hit once for the same reason).

**Real cost across v1 + v2**: roughly $26 total for this whole exploration
(v1's ~$24 on Standard tier including one run whose paid clips were lost to
the ffmpeg-missing bug documented in the earlier entry, plus ~$1.60 for v2's
Lite-tier iteration). **Final v2 result, confirmed by Dev watching it**: a
clean 16.0s, 720x1280, no-black-bars reel with natural-paced worker motion --
approved as the visual baseline to build on, not yet approved as a finished
format.

**v3 -- prepared for FUTURE runs, explicitly NOT generated yet.** Dev gave
three directions for what comes next, all implemented in code but
deliberately left un-triggered:

1. **Model tier: switch to `veo-3.1-fast-generate-001` for all future runs**,
   with audio back ON. Researched (not assumed) that Fast genuinely supports
   native audio generation, unlike some cheaper tiers -- real cost estimate
   researched at ~$0.10-0.15/s, so ~$1.60-$2.40 for a 16s (4x4s) reel, still
   5-7x cheaper than v1's Standard tier while getting real audio back.
2. **ASMR audio, done properly this time.** v1's approach was a single vague
   prose paragraph ("ASMR-style renovation sound design") appended to every
   prompt -- gave the model nothing concrete to render. Researched Google
   Cloud's own official "Ultimate prompting guide for Veo 3.1" (2026) and
   adopted its documented audio cue syntax instead: `SFX: ...` for discrete
   sound effects (the scrape of a dustpan, a paint tin lid popping, the
   crinkle of plastic wrap being pulled off furniture) and `Ambient noise:
   ...` for background atmosphere, one specific set per clip rather than one
   generic paragraph reused everywhere. Also adopted the guide's five-part
   prompt structure -- Cinematography + Subject + Action + Context + Style/
   Ambiance -- with explicit camera language ("Static locked-off shot") now
   stated up front rather than implied.
3. **More transformation "wow factor."** `generate_before()` escalated from a
   mild "unfinished construction site" (v1/v2) to genuine abandoned-building
   decay: collapsed ceiling section with exposed joists, large water stains,
   plaster crumbled to bare lath, a cracked window pane, a rubble pile, mold.
   Deliberately kept the window wall and fireplace opening recognizable
   throughout -- those are the anchors the whole 5-image chain depends on to
   still read as the same room; everything else was fair game to wreck.
   `demo`'s description was updated to match (early cleanup now deals with
   rubble and a tarped ceiling, not just dust).

**Other Veo 3.1 prompting findings from the same research, not yet applied
but worth knowing for later**: dialogue goes in quotes attached to a speaker
(not needed here -- no dialogue in this format); negative framing should be
avoided in favor of affirmative description (same rule already established
for BFL FLUX elsewhere in this repo, now confirmed to also hold for Veo, not
just BFL); "timestamp prompting" (`[00:00-00:02] ... [00:02-00:04] ...` within
a single prompt) can direct a full multi-beat sequence in ONE generation
call rather than chaining several -- not used here since the 5-keyframe/
4-clip structure already solves the same pacing problem a different way, but
worth considering if this format's clip count ever needs to shrink for cost
reasons.

**Status: code is ready, nothing has been generated against it.** The next
real run against `veo-3.1-fast-generate-001` with the new audio cues and the
escalated `before` prompt is what will actually validate all three v3 changes
-- don't assume any of them work as described until that run happens and gets
reviewed the same way v1 and v2 were.

## E-Series: upscale adopted as standard, naming fixed, e1-02/e1-03/e1-04/e1-05 (2026-08-22/23)

Catching this file up on three real commits that shipped without an llms.txt
update at the time (`552a828`, `175b9c1`, plus today's `e73ef32` + the image
commit after it) -- a gap against the standing "update llms.txt every run"
rule, worth flagging rather than quietly backfilling. Consolidating all of it
here in one entry since it's one continuous thread.

**Upscale+sharpen adopted as the permanent pipeline step.** Following the
"why lower quality" investigation above, Dev asked to see the upscale
comparison applied to already-generated images before deciding, reviewed it,
and confirmed: "wait this all happened with code, that looks amazing, we
will follow this route." Wired into `generate_room()` itself in
`concept_tools/generate_eseries.py` (`upscale_and_sharpen()`) -- Lanczos
resize from 768x1344 up to FLUX's own 1088x1920, plus a mild
`ImageFilter.UnsharpMask`, both from Pillow. Dev then asked directly whether
this consumed any AI credits: confirmed no -- it's pure local CPU image
processing on bytes already returned by the one paid Gemini call, zero
additional API calls, zero additional cost. `image_size="4K"` was dropped
from the generation request since it's confirmed to have zero effect on this
model. e1-01's three files were replaced with their upscaled versions.

**Naming convention fixed after Dev uploaded more reference reels.** More
"Type 1 - firstchair" reels revealed real style/mood diversity even within
one type (different color grades, wildly different cut pacing -- one video a
32-cut flash-montage in 7.4s). Dev pointed out e1-01's filenames
(`e1-01_liv_app.png`) didn't self-document which images share a style well
enough to "match similar images together to make a reel" once multiple
sets/moods exist. Fixed: every set now carries a required top-level
`style_slug`, and room file stems follow `{set_id}_{room}_{style_slug}`,
matching the a-d series' own `{concept}_{room}_{stylename}` pattern exactly
(e.g. `d01_lib_oxblood`). e1-01's 3 committed files were renamed to match.
Also added a per-set `light_sentence` override (`build_room_prompt` falls
back to `ROOM_LIGHT` when absent) so new sets can capture genuinely
different lighting moods instead of every set forcing Dev's established
blue-hour treatment -- e1-01 itself is unaffected (no override set).

**e1-02 ("warmvintage", from reel 6) and e1-03 ("sagecoastal", from reel 4)
generated, upscaled, uploaded to Drive, and approved by Dev** ("I approve").
e1-02: soft warm hazy vintage-film grade, Spanish-colonial-leaning styling
(carved walnut/mahogany, terracotta tile, checkerboard textiles), living
room + entry hallway. e1-03: bright Mediterranean-coastal daylight (sage
cabinetry, travertine, brass), kitchen + dining room.

**Dev's next feedback: all sets so far read as too bright, wanted real
dark/moody variety plus a special exterior-to-interior "house tour" set,
grounded in actual research rather than invention** -- exact ask: "why are
all images so bright... add such to the mix too, also create one that shows
one exterior and rest interior for a special kinda reel that's kinda gives
whole house tour... research online and see what kinda theme and mood I am
looking for and whats going viral currently on tiktok and instagram."

Handled by going back through PREVIOUSLY-DOWNLOADED but not-yet-reviewed
reference frames (from the earlier `analyze_reference_reels.py` run) rather
than inventing a dark mood from scratch: reel 4 -- the same reel e1-03's
bright sage kitchen came from -- has a second, genuinely dark frame later in
the same video (near-black cabinetry, brass hardware, marble, dark wood
beams), captioned "This is why cabinet color matters" (the reel is a
bright-vs-dark cabinet-color comparison, not one single mood; only its
bright half had been sampled into e1-03). Reel 5 shows the same dark
cabinet-kitchen mood again. That real frame is e1-04's actual grounding.
Cross-checked against two live WebSearches (not assumed): "moody organic
modern" (dark wood, earthy deep tones, warm dramatic lighting) confirmed as
a real current 2026 trend; house-tour/room-flow content confirmed as a
recognized popular reel format, supporting the exterior->interior structure
Dev asked for.

**e1-04 ("darkmoody")**: kitchen + primary bedroom, deep near-black
cabinetry/millwork, marble, aged brass, dark oak beams, photographed at
night lit only by the room's own warm brass fixtures -- high-contrast,
near-black shadow with deliberate warm light pools, dramatic rather than
cozy.

**e1-05 ("quietluxury")**: the exterior->interior house-tour set -- front
exterior facade, entry foyer, living room, warm-neutral "quiet luxury"
palette (greige limestone/render, walnut, aged brass, linen/boucle),
golden-hour directional light throughout. Required new prompt-composition
handling: `COMPOSITION`/`SPATIAL_RULE` (imported from `generate_concept.py`)
are written specifically for interior three-quarter room views and don't
fit a building facade. Added `EXTERIOR_COMPOSITION`/`EXTERIOR_SPATIAL_RULE`
constants and a per-room `is_exterior` flag; `build_room_prompt()` now
branches on it (`Exterior photograph of...` vs `Interior photograph of...`,
different composition/spatial language). This is the first exterior shot
this generator has ever produced.

Both sets generated one test room first (kit for e1-04, ext for e1-05),
reviewed by eye before generating the rest -- same discipline as every prior
e-series batch. All 5 images (e1-04: kit, bed; e1-05: ext, ent, liv)
confirmed clean by eye: e1-04 genuinely dark and dramatic (not just "less
bright"), e1-05's exterior geometrically coherent (no floating/
interpenetrating architecture) and its entry/living room continue the same
warm walnut palette as the exterior, with a staircase visible in both
interior shots reinforcing the house-tour flow. Committed to
`assets/application_eseries/`, uploaded to Drive via
`upload-eseries-to-drive.yml` under "E-Series Generated Output/e1-04" and
"/e1-05". **Awaiting Dev's approval before any further batch**, same
checkpoint pattern Dev has now established twice.

## E-Series: "old money" is now the default look, per Dev's real reference reels (2026-08-23)

Dev approved e1-04/e1-05 but called the e-series overall "dull and boring"
and asked for genuine "old money" wow factor, "not too bright" -- and this
time sent two real reference videos rather than a mood word, explicitly:
"for next few generations only stick to this." Downloaded both via a new
one-off `download-drive-files.yml` (fetches specific Drive file IDs, not a
whole folder -- existing tooling only handled folder listing) and sampled
frames locally with the ffmpeg already installed on this machine, rather
than guessing at the look from Dev's description alone.

**What the references actually show, not assumed:** both are "ANB
Architecture Studio" branded kitchen-design reels. Reel 1: a "MATERIAL
PALETTE" branding montage -- swatch cards (charcoal plaster/black marble/
walnut/aged brass; warm ivory/cream marble/walnut/brass; slate/walnut/cream
marble/brass; deep maroon/olive green/walnut/cream quartz -- each combo used
in ONE finished kitchen, not layered together) intercut with the finished
kitchens: every one built around a dramatic waterfall-edge stone island,
2-3 slim cylindrical aged-brass pendants at staggered heights, dark walnut
cabinetry, glass-front upper cabinets with their own interior lighting,
warm layered ambient light (never sun-bright, never night-dark). Reel 2: a
heritage/English-country-manor kitchen -- antique double-dome brass
pendant, dramatic veined-marble waterfall island on a dark oak base, woven
rush counter stools, brass bridge faucet, hung copper pans, a gilt-framed
oil landscape painting, a stoneware jug with foraged olive branches, linen
café curtains, soft diffused daylight. **Both genuinely sparse on
styling** -- 2-3 objects per shot -- which is itself a likely real reason
the earlier e-series sets read as "trying too hard": density was reading
as effort, not luxury, compared to these.

**New mechanism added, not just a new set:** `styling_restraint_sentence`,
an optional per-set field in `concept_tools/generate_eseries.py` appended
after `STYLING_RULE` in `build_room_prompt()` -- added because
`STYLING_RULE` alone (shared with the a-d series, "a small number of
larger, well-spaced pieces") reads looser than what these references
actually show. e1-06's version caps styling at "two or three objects in
the whole frame."

**e1-06 ("oldmoney") built and iterated on a real defect, not shipped on
the first try:** dark walnut cabinetry/millwork, dramatically veined
cream-and-grey waterfall marble, aged brass, warm soft-plaster walls; warm
layered ambient light_sentence (pendant glow + under-cabinet + cove light,
moderate exposure throughout, explicitly neither sun-bright nor
night-dark) written from what the references show rather than reusing
`ROOM_LIGHT`'s blue-hour treatment, since neither reference shows blue
dusk at the windows.

**First kitchen test render had two real, visible defects, caught by eye
before committing anything:** (1) the palette_sentence's own vague
"occasional deep bottle-green or oxblood accents used sparingly" clause
got rendered as a whole out-of-palette green cabinet run, not a small
accent -- root cause was the word "sparingly" giving the model no concrete
scale to work with, and the accent detail wasn't even load-bearing (my own
addition, not a specific thing either reference showed), so it was
dropped entirely rather than reworded. (2) An unscripted second table with
its own citrus bowl appeared disconnected in the extreme foreground --
root cause: the kitchen's styling text never stated the island was the
room's only furniture, so the model invented one to satisfy COMPOSITION's
generic "a piece of furniture in the near foreground" clause. Fixed by
adding an explicit, affirmative statement to the kitchen's own styling
text that the island is "the sole piece of furniture standing in the
room." Regenerated once: both defects gone, confirmed by eye -- single
consistent palette, no orphaned objects, island genuinely reads as the
"wow factor" hero the reference material shows. Dining room generated
fresh afterward (gilt-framed oil landscape, brass linear chandelier,
walnut table, stoneware jug with olive branches) and reads as the same
house as the kitchen through a shared archway -- no separate fix needed.
